beats.title: One payment, one question
beats.narration: Start with a payment for eighty-four fifty at North Market. We want to predict whether it will later be disputed. The amount and merchant are available now; the dispute outcome arrives later.

beats.title: Describe the fields
beats.narration: Describe that record with a small RelFlow model. Number handles the amount, Category handles the merchant, and Boolean handles the yes-or-no outcome. The parent keywords give each field its name.

beats.title: Keep the answer out of the input
beats.narration: The important option is mask equals true. The observed dispute label supplies the training answer, but its content never becomes an input. The model must learn from evidence available before that outcome.

beats.title: Train, then ask about a new payment
beats.narration: Train on earlier payments and validate on a later period. For a new request, supply amount and merchant and omit disputed. Next, add earlier transactions to give this same prediction more context.

beats.title: The payment has a past
beats.narration: A payment often makes more sense beside earlier transactions from the same account. Add a recent transactions list to the record. Each transaction keeps its age, amount, and merchant together as one historical event.

beats.title: Describe repeated records
beats.narration: A Branch describes those repeated records. Its children describe the values in each transaction. Add this named branch to the payment model; amount, merchant, and the hidden dispute target stay at the payment level.

beats.title: Keep the most recent history
beats.narration: Prepare history in oldest-to-newest order. Length thirty-two caps the collection, and tail keeps the last thirty-two supplied records when it overflows. An account with no earlier transactions has an empty history list.

beats.title: Respect the prediction moment
beats.narration: Every historical record must already be known before the current payment. Sorting and that cutoff belong in application preparation. Training and prediction use the same nested shape; prediction requests still omit only the dispute target.
lines: Use the same preparation for every split

beats.title: Names connect schema and records
beats.narration: RelFlow reads the names and nesting declared in the schema. Amount reads the current payment amount; merchant reads its merchant. The recent transactions branch reads the list, and each child reads within its own transaction.

beats.title: Keep application metadata
beats.narration: A record can also carry application metadata such as a payment identifier. Extra columns do not become model inputs automatically. Keep them for preparation or retain them with predictions when your application needs to match results back.

beats.title: Prepare the shape before binding
beats.narration: When source names or shapes differ, use queries or preprocessing deliberately. Preparation can rename fields, derive ages, join history, and apply the time cutoff. A missing required input is a binding error; an explicit null follows its field contract.

beats.title: Supply your prepared Arrow splits
beats.narration: Pass independent, application-supplied Arrow tables to the data module. Those records supply observed dispute labels for training and validation. Prediction uses the same preparation, with the directly bound supervised target omitted from new requests.

beats.title: Learn from earlier payments
beats.narration: Start with the payment model and its hidden dispute target. Prepare independent training and validation splits from your application. Earlier payments teach the model; later observations help select the model state to keep.

beats.title: Connect the data module
beats.narration: The Arrow data module connects those prepared tables to the model. It does not invent application records or evaluation boundaries. Keep the schema, history cutoff, and preparation consistent across both supplied splits.

beats.title: Configure the run on fit
beats.narration: Set batch size and AdamW options on fit. Batch size is per device. Early stopping and rollback monitor validation loss by default, and fitting returns with the best validation checkpoint restored. These settings are starting choices to evaluate.

beats.title: Distinguish a new fit from a resumed run
beats.narration: Each ordinary fit binds a fresh optimizer to the current parameters; supply any scheduler for that run. Save an artifact for model state. Full continuation, including optimizer and loop progress, requires a full checkpoint passed through checkpoint path.
lines: Model.save: schema and learned model state
Full checkpoint + ckpt_path: resume a run

beats.title: Ask about an unseen outcome
beats.narration: After training, request a prediction for a payment whose dispute outcome is unknown. Supply the fields visible at payment time and omit disputed. The payment identifier is application metadata, useful for connecting the answer to its request.

beats.title: Return an Arrow table
beats.narration: Predict returns an Arrow table with inputs and predictions columns. Retain explicitly selects processed source columns to copy into inputs. Without postprocessing, each output row corresponds to one processed observation; retention does not change model inputs.
lines: # request_table is supplied by your application.

beats.title: Read the target by its address
beats.narration: Inside predictions, the literal slash-prefixed field disputed identifies this target. Its content contains the probability of true. The code selects nested Arrow struct fields rather than treating the output as a flat column of labels.

beats.title: Read the flags with the value
beats.narration: State describes value-state probabilities, and inferred says reconstruction was requested at that position. It is not a confidence score. This schematic shows placeholders instead of measured predictions; choose application decisions and evaluate their quality on held-out observations.

beats.title: One observation has a tree
beats.narration: The schema describes one observation. A payment has ordinary amount and merchant fields, a repeated history branch, and a dispute target. Each historical transaction keeps its own age, amount, and merchant together at the same position.

beats.title: Context follows the structure
beats.narration: The history branch builds context from those transactions. The root combines that context with the current payment. Tree connections describe ownership and information structure; application preparation performs the database joins that assembled this observation.
lines: Payment root: combine current and past

beats.title: Names become addresses
beats.narration: Parent keywords name the children. The root itself is anonymous, at slash; payment is only the diagram label. Construct nested addresses with one argument per component. Addresses identify schema locations in predictions, metrics, and schema edits.

beats.title: Choose a practical history limit
beats.narration: The example caps history at thirty-two records and keeps the tail of oldest-to-newest input. This is an application choice, separate from model size. Repeated fields and their padding still cost memory, so evaluate capacity with realistic histories.
lines: length=32: hard cap on retained history
Model size and collection size are separate
Repeated fields and padding consume memory

beats.title: Visibility and learning are separate choices
beats.narration: A mask controls what the model can see and what it learns to predict. Those are separate effects. For a supervised dispute target, mask equals true hides the input content and uses its observed value as the training answer.

beats.title: Dropout does not create an objective
beats.narration: A floating-point mask rate supplies training-only input dropout. Without reconstruction, hiding an amount does not ask the model to predict it. The fifteen-percent rate shown here is an illustrative configuration choice, not a measured performance result.

beats.title: Request sampled reconstruction explicitly
beats.narration: An explicit Mask with reconstruct equals true adds an objective for selected observed values. The remaining visible context must explain the hidden amount. Fractional reconstruction samples during training and evaluation, but is inactive during ordinary prediction.

beats.title: Choose learned masking or structural removal
beats.narration: A learned mask keeps a present coordinate while hiding its value. Skip removes that input representation from encoder attention. Reconstruction still keeps the pristine answer for loss. Branch policies share a decision across descendants; selectors can target particular records.
lines: Learned mask: hide value, retain coordinate
Branch policy: share selection with descendants

beats.title: Export learned context
beats.narration: An embedding is a numeric representation of learned context. Set embed equals true at the model root to export the payment representation. The hidden dispute target still supplies the learning objective; exporting a vector creates no objective by itself.

beats.title: Choose the location deliberately
beats.narration: You can also export a history branch summary or a leaf's pooled decoder context. With the extra-small preset's single reduction output, a history branch export gives one summary per payment, rather than one vector per transaction.
lines: xs history export: one summary per payment

beats.title: Read the root representation
beats.narration: Prediction output stores requested embeddings at schema addresses. Slash selects the anonymous root, and embedding selects its vector. Exported vectors are float thirty-two and normalized along their feature axis; an all-zero vector remains zero.

beats.title: Evaluate the downstream use
beats.narration: A good dispute predictor does not establish good similarity or clustering. Evaluate embeddings on the application task and preserve the trained schema and state. Supervised labels and sampled reconstruction can both teach context; choose the learning signal explicitly.

beats.title: Learn from records without task labels
beats.narration: Pretraining is optional. Historical amounts and merchants can provide their own supervision before dispute labels exist. Hide selected observed values, then learn to reconstruct them from remaining context. Keep held-out accounts and future observations out of training.

beats.title: Use a reconstruction policy
beats.narration: Put an explicit reconstruction mask on historical fields, then fit with independent Arrow splits and save the model artifact. This fifteen-percent sampling rate is illustrative configuration, not a performance claim. Plain dropout would create no pretraining objective.

beats.title: Adapt the saved model to disputes
beats.narration: Load the artifact, remove sampled reconstruction from historical inputs, and add the hidden dispute target. Compatible state transfers; the new target starts freshly initialized. Keep existing addresses and geometry stable when reusing the learned model.

beats.title: Start a new optimization run
beats.narration: Fine-tune on labeled splits with a fresh optimizer and any scheduler supplied for this run. This is a new task, not full checkpoint continuation. Compare against supervised training from scratch on the same held-out task; pretraining does not guarantee improvement.
lines: Pretrained model state + new dispute target
Labeled Arrow splits: a new fit
